newsitem.title: UK: UK gilts this week-U.S., UK rate rise risk dominates.
newsitem.headline: UK gilts this week-U.S., UK rate rise risk dominates.

text.p: The UK gilt market has little chance of independent action this week despite speculation of another rise in Britain's 6.75 percent interest rates on Thursday.
"Gilts are firmly under to cosh of (U.S.) Treasuries and they're going to drag us around this week like they did last," one senior UK gilt salesman at a UK brokerage said.

Soaring optimism that the U.S. economy was enjoying strong growth with low inflation pushed T-bonds higher last week, dragging gilts up to a new contract high. But by the end of the week strong payroll figures and a leap in the July NAPM index sent international bonds sharply lower.
LIFFE September gilts lost 17/32 at 114-29/32 on Friday and fell a further 7/32 at 114-22/32 on Monday.
"The market was pretty thin on Friday and there's a chance that the move was an exaggerated one," said Societe Generale strategist Adrian Davies. "People are waiting to see what happens in the U.S."

The U.S. market has little significant data to get through this week but does face the start of quarterly refunding auctions, with the Treasury set to auction $16.0 billion in three-year notes on Tuesday, $12.0 billion of 10-year notes on Wednesday and then $10.0 billion of 30-year bonds the following week.

On the domestic front, the August 6 and 7 meeting of the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) takes centre stage. A Reuter survey of 23 economists suggests that on balance the markets should be bracing themselves for the fourth 1/4 rate rise since May -- only 7 of those surveyed expect interest rates to stay unchanged.

HSBC economists expect rates to rise as the central bank continues its bid to squeeze inflation pressures out of the system but argue that the market has gone a long way to discounting such a move already, leaving gilts well supported against their European counterparts in the short term.
Fresh worries about the possibility of a switch by the Bundesbank to variable rate repos during its summer recess have depressed Bund market sentiment, according to HSBC bond strategist Philip Tyson.
"Although we believe that these concerns are misplaced, they have weighed on Bunds...and more than offset persistent UK interest rate fears, he said.

"As a result, domestic concerns in the UK are unlikely to lead to any widening in the 10-year gilt/Bund spread in the immediate future...Risks appear skewed in favour of a move towards 140 basis points in the near term," he said.
The gilt/Bund spread widened out to 152 on Monday from 147 on Friday but dealers said there was good support around 160 basis points.
Societe Generale's Davies argues that if the MPC opts to raise rates, this will actually boost the allure of long-dated gilts because of the perception that inflation pressures are being checked.

The market has little in the way of official data to focus upon with industrial production for June, due at 0830 GMT on Tuesday, the main release. It is expected to show a monthly rise of 0.4 percent in manufacturing compared with the previous month and a 1.2 percent growth rate compared with a year earlier. But is considered too historical to hold much sway.

Instead, the distributive trades survey for July from the Confederation of British Industry, due at 0900 GMT on Thursday, is likely to be the main indicator even if its correlation with the official sales series has been erratic in recent months.

"In line with other indicators of the depth and breadth of the consumer recovery, the July report should underpin the general sentiment regarding buoyant consumer activity," Morgan Grenfell economists said in their Week Ahead report.

British consumers have been the main engine of economic growth in the UK with their spending power having received a massive boost of around 35 billion stg from building society flotations. They indulged in a spending orgy in June and analysts are looking to see whether this abated in July.
